newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA LEFTIST OPPOSITION SLAMS RULING CENTRISTS.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA LEFTIST OPPOSITION SLAMS RULING CENTRISTS.

text.p: Romania's former ruling leftists on Tuesday accused the government of pursuing "authoritarian policies" aimed at intimidating parliamentary opposition.

In a letter to reformist President Emil Constantinescu, his ex-communist predecessor Ion Iliescu slammed the centrist government over its reform policies and complained of purging in the state administration.

"The authoritarian and arrogant behaviour of the majority coalition threatens to install a dictatorship of the majority and to sideline the opposition," Iliescu red out the letter at a news conference of his Party of Social Democracy (PDSR).
The coalition government took office after elections last November when Iliescu and his PDSR lost their seven-year grip on power.
Tuesday's accusations followed a walk-out from parliament late on Monday staged by Iliescu and fellow PDSR MPs over last week's vote in parliament to strip an opposition senatore of his immunity.
Iliescu, now a member of parliament's upper Senate house said the walk-out -- which followed an opposition motion on farming policies rejected earlier this month -- fell short of a boycott.
"We will not obstruct parliament," Iliescu told the news conference. "But we either advance towards a state of law with a real democracy or we turn into a state dominated by the present coalition."
Romania is lobbying to join the European Union and enter NATO in a first wave of enlargment when the Alliance announces its first eastward expansion at a July summit in Madrid.
With market reforms trailing since communism collapsed in 1989, the government has launched tough measures to put the economy back on track.
Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's coalition -- including Christian and Social Democrats and representatives of Romania's large ethnic Hungarian community -- has a comfortable majority in parliament.

Short-term steps focus on a package of some 50 laws, including the 1997 state budget, a plank for Romania's hopes of renewed credits from international lenders, which have to go through parliament for approval. REUTER
